title: London plans
summary: The London is one set-up for many games: Bf4, e3, Nf3, Bd3, c3. Then use Ne5, keep your bishop, and aim at the kingside.
body:
### The London set-up

The London is a plan, not a list of moves to learn. You play the same set-up against many openings. You make the same pawn and piece moves, so you know where everything goes.

The set-up has five parts:

- **Bf4 first.** Bring the c1 bishop out before you play e3. After e3 the bishop is shut in.
- **e3, c3 and Nf3.** The c3 and e3 pawns both guard the d4 pawn. The knight on f3 guards d4.
- **Bd3 and Nbd2.** The bishop on d3 aims at the black kingside. The second knight goes to d2. Then you castle.
- **Ne5.** A knight on e5 is strong. It is an outpost only when no black pawn can attack it (lesson 14). Your d4 pawn and your bishop support it. Check that no black pawn can kick it away.
- **Keep your bishop.** Black often attacks your bishop on f4. For example, ...Bd6 hits it, or ...Nh5 hits it. Against ...Bd6, step back to g3. Against ...Nh5, play h3 in advance, so the bishop can go to h2.

Why keep the bishop? It stands outside your pawns and guards e5, the square for your knight. When you trade it for a knight, your plan is weaker.

When your pieces are ready, you can attack the kingside. The bishop on d3 and the knight on e5 aim at it. Do not attack with only one piece.

Do not move kingside pawns before your pieces are out, except h3 to save your bishop. And look at what your opponent threatens. The London is safe, but it does not play itself.

The exercises use positions from your London repertoire. Find the set-up move in each one.

Rule of thumb: bishop out before e3, bishop to d3, knight to e5, and keep your bishop.

exercises.prompt: White to move. Develop your dark-squared bishop outside the pawn chain.
exercises.explanation: Bf4 brings the bishop out before e3 shuts it in. This is the key London move.

exercises.prompt: White to move. Support your d4 pawn and your f4 bishop with a pawn.
exercises.explanation: The e3 pawn guards d4 and f4. It also opens the diagonal for your f1 bishop.

exercises.prompt: White to move. Put a knight on a strong central square.
exercises.explanation: Ne5 is supported by the d4 pawn and the bishop on f4. It attacks the c6 knight, which has no guard. The d5 pawn has passed d6, and the f7 pawn can only kick it after the f6 knight moves. It also points at the kingside.

exercises.prompt: White to move. Black's bishop attacks yours. Step back and keep your bishop.
exercises.explanation: Bg3 keeps your bishop on the b8-h2 diagonal, and Bg5 also keeps it. If Black plays ...Bxg3, retake with hxg3: the h-file is then half open for your rook. If you leave the bishop on f4, ...Bxf4 exf4 doubles your f-pawns.

exercises.prompt: White to move. Prepare a retreat square for your f4 bishop.
exercises.explanation: h3 gives the bishop the h2 square. After ...Nh5 you play Bh2 and keep your bishop. Without h3, ...Nh5 usually forces you to trade it or lose time.

exercises.prompt: White to move. Develop your light-squared bishop so that it aims at the black kingside.
exercises.explanation: Bd3 aims along the diagonal at h7 and gets the bishop out so you can castle. Be2 and Bb5 develop too, but they do not aim at the kingside.
